title: The Brain Paradox: Losing One Brain Spot Freezes Tea Like Ice
description:
Behavioral & Circuit Analysis — Josef Zihl (1983): Akinetopsia ('Motion Blindness') — Why Patient L.M. Saw Pouring Tea Freeze Like a Solid Glacier, grounded in J. Zihl, D. Von Cramon, N. Mai (1983) (Brain). Empirical findings show that in October 1978, a 43-year-old woman in Munich (Patient L.M.) suffered a rare bilateral superior sagittal sinus venous stroke affecting symmetrical patches of lateral temporo-occipital cortex (human V5 / hMT+) on BOTH sides of her brain — and walked into Josef Zihl's Max Planck clinic with a complaint neurology had almost never heard.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how primary visual cortex, temporal lobe, auditory cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that her color vision was 100% normal, her static reading acuity and stereo depth perception were completely intact, and she named stationary objects effortlessly — yet smooth visual motion had vanished from her universe.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- J. Zihl, D. Von Cramon, N. Mai (1983). SELECTIVE DISTURBANCE OF MOVEMENT VISION AFTER BILATERAL BRAIN DAMAGE. Brain. https://doi.org/10.1093/brain/106.2.313
- J. Zihl, D. Von Cramon, N. Mai, CH. Schmid (1991). DISTURBANCE OF MOVEMENT VISION AFTER BILATERAL POSTERIOR BRAIN DAMAGE: FURTHER EVIDENCE AND FOLLOW UP OBSERVATIONS. Brain. https://doi.org/10.1093/brain/114.5.2235
- S. Zeki (1991). CEREBRAL AKINETOPSIA (VISUAL MOTION BLINDNESS). Brain. https://doi.org/10.1093/brain/114.2.811

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
